title: Validation check
description:
One thing that must be true before a task can pass a gate (plan §6).

A packet used to carry `validation: ["npm test"]` — a string nobody ran, checked against nothing, satisfied by remembering to. A check instead names itself (`checkId`), says how it is satisfied (`kind`), and says when it is required (`requiredAt`), which is what lets a gate ask a question with an answer.

The plan lives inside the frozen, digested half of the task packet. That is the load-bearing property: an Agent cannot add a check that passes, drop one that fails, or edit the command it is judged by without restating the task under a new generation, which is visible. What freezing buys is integrity, not safety — it proves the command run is the one the author wrote, and a frozen `rm -rf` is still `rm -rf`. So `command` is structured `argv`, spawned without a shell: no word splitting, no globbing, no `&&`, no `$(...)`, and no quoting rules for an author to get wrong. A plan that genuinely needs shell syntax asks for it by name as `shell-command`, so the capability is legible in the frozen packet and in review instead of being handed to every check by default.

The kinds are deliberately one vocabulary rather than separate mechanisms. A test run and a human judgement are both semantic evidence about one candidate, both go stale when the candidate or the inputs move, and a gate has to weigh them together (plan §7). A `review` check is answered by looking at review decisions (`reviewStateFor`), not by recording a second copy of the judgement as evidence.

The branches are closed objects rather than one open shape, so a `role` on a command check, a `command` on an argv check, or a `timeoutMs` on a review check is refused instead of ignored. A field that is silently dropped is worse than a rejected one: the author believes they constrained something they did not.

checkId.description: Names this check within its task, and therefore names its evidence. Kebab-case and unique in the plan: two checks sharing an id would make "unit-tests passed" ambiguous about which unit tests, and a gate would accept either.

requiredAt.description: The gates that demand this check. At least one, because a check required nowhere is a note. Gates rather than a single "must pass" flag because the same task wants different evidence at different moments — a fast unit run before handing off, the full suite before merge — and demanding everything at every step is how the step gets skipped.

description.description: What this check is for, in the author's words. For the Agent that has to decide whether a failure is worth escalating; `npm test -- coupon` does not say why.

timeoutMs.description: How long the check gets before it is abandoned as `errored`. Omitted means the runner's default. A timeout is not a failure: nothing was learned about the candidate.

commandCheck.description: Satisfied by running a program and recording what happened. Spawned as argv with no shell, which is the default because it is the weaker capability: a check that only needs to run a test suite does not need word splitting, redirection or command substitution to do it.

argv.description: The program and its arguments, already split into words: ["npm", "test", "--", "coupon"], not "npm test -- coupon". No shell parses this, so a word containing spaces or quotes arrives at the program exactly as written — which is the point, and also why `argv[0]` must be a program rather than a command line. On Windows a launcher such as npm or npx is a `.cmd` batch file that cannot be spawned without a shell; name the executable it wraps, or declare the check as `shell-command`.

shellCommandCheck.description: Satisfied the same way as a `command` check, but the line is handed to a shell — pipelines, `&&`, redirection and substitution all work. A separate kind rather than a flag on `command` so that the extra capability is a word a reviewer sees while reading the plan, not a boolean buried in a check body. Reach for it when the check genuinely is a shell line; for anything else `command` says more by being able to do less.

command.description: The shell line, run in the task's worktree. One string rather than argv because a shell line is one string: splitting it into words here and reassembling it there would be a second, worse shell.

reviewCheck.description: Satisfied by somebody in a named role approving this candidate. Answered from recorded review decisions, which is what makes it go stale the same way a test result does.

role.description: The capacity the approval must be given in. A role rather than a subject: naming a person makes the plan unsatisfiable the moment that Agent's session ends, and the point of the check is independence, not a particular reviewer.
